summary:
Reading edition B (spec/tarn.md) into edition A (scratch/cleanroom/editions/a/tarn.md) to find additions -- content B decides that A does not -- I found none across all 24 sections and 8 appendices. A diff -q pass over every section (after splitting each edition by heading line ranges) showed that sections 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 19, 20 and 24 are byte-identical between the two editions, so there is zero addition risk there: the readable rewrite has not yet touched them. Sections 1 through 8, which the git history confirms are the sections actively being rewritten, show the expected pattern throughout: B is a shorter, differently-ordered restatement of A, never a wider or newer one. Every passage in B that initially looked unique -- found via diff hunks that showed only B-side lines with no A-side counterpart -- turned out, on a distinctive-fragment grep against the other file, to already exist in A, either in the same section (reworded) or relocated to a different section. Three such relocations were verified directly: (1) B's sections 2 and 3 are swapped in physical file order (Terminology before Conformance) while each keeps its canonical section number, a purely structural reorder; (2) the metadata-compression/quarantine passage moves from early in A's section 7 to a position near B's 7.4, with every clause preserved; (3) the list of grounds on which a verifier reports cannot-establish moves from A's section 2.3 to B's section 21.6, with B's 2.3 left pointing at a forward reference in its place. Five cross-reference numbers were updated to track relocation (2) and are not separate findings. One wording change -- A's "the per-channel value" shortened to B's "the value" in the fill-value definition -- does not widen or narrow the defined term once both sentences' channel-scoping language is compared. I did not find any Note/Example/Rationale-only carried normative content unique to B, any register-row, term, table or fenced-block difference (out of scope per the mechanical checker), or any consequence B draws that A's own text does not already license. The findings below are therefore all EQUIVALENT (verified relocations/rewordings), recorded for the maintainer's visibility; no LOSS, ADDITION, CONTRADICTION or AMBIGUITY survived the check.</summary>

findings.title: Metadata-compression/quarantine paragraph relocated within section 7, not lost or added
findings.detail: Edition A states the rule that metadata compression exists only at record granularity and that user metadata is quarantined early in section 7, right after the directory-region CRC rule. Edition B states the identical rule, same extent-length floor, same encoding values, same quarantine scope and SHOULD-report, same carve-out, same resource-decline exception, but positioned just before section 7.4 the layer record instead. No clause was dropped or added, only its position in the section moved, and cross-references to it elsewhere were updated from 7.1 to 7.3 to track the move.
findings.quotation_a: Metadata compression exists only at record granularity. Each user-metadata record carries its document in its extent, never inline, and declares the document's encoding in its own inline payload (u8: 0 invalid, 1 = none, 2 = zstd; section 18).
findings.quotation_b: Metadata compression exists only at record granularity: the directory and the tile-index region are always raw (the index so that it can be range-fetched, section 15), and tile payloads use the layer's codec field (section 17). Each user-metadata record carries its document in its extent, never inline, and declares the document's encoding in its own inline payload (u8: 0 invalid, 1 = none, 2 = zstd; section 18).
findings.byte_level_rationale: Same rule, same requirement ID and same sub-clauses in both editions; an implementation built from either text alone enforces identical bytes and identical accept/reject behavior for user-metadata records. Only the paragraph's position within section 7 and a few cross-reference numbers elsewhere changed.

findings.title: Verifier's cannot-establish grounds list relocated from section 2.3 to section 21, not added
findings.detail: Edition A spells out, inline in section 2.3's conforming-verifier bullet, the five grounds on which a verifier reports cannot-establish: unimplemented format major, an MU=1 record of unimplemented type, cannot execute a codec or filter, resource decline on a layer's or tile's decode, declines to decode a user-metadata document. Edition B's section 2.3 shortens this to a forward pointer naming section 21.6, and states the identical five-ground list, same citations, in section 21 instead. This is the same content at a different address, not a new decision in section 21.
findings.quotation_a: when the file names a format major version it does not implement, when a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement, when it cannot execute a codec or filter, when it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check the decoded-content obligations, or when it declines to decode a user-metadata document.
findings.quotation_b: A verifier is unable to check a requirement on a capability or resource ground, and so reports cannot establish, as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement, it cannot execute a codec or filter, it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check the decoded-content obligations, or it declines to decode a user-metadata document.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Same five grounds, same requirement citations, same verdict in both editions; a verifier built from either text alone recognizes the same situations and reports the same verdict. Only the section that states them differs.
